vignette:
Omar is a 40-year-old software engineer, married, who works for a mid-sized tech firm in a glass-and-steel office building. Two years ago, a severe earthquake struck during the workday, collapsing a section of his floor. He spent six hours pinned under a concrete beam, conscious the entire time, listening to the groaning of metal, the screams of colleagues trapped around him, and the frantic calls of rescue workers. He was eventually pulled out with a fractured leg and a concussion, and spent several weeks in hospital. The earthquake was officially a natural disaster, but Omar has since become convinced that his building’s owner—and specifically the project manager who had cut corners on seismic reinforcements—was directly responsible for the deaths that day. He now ruminates almost obsessively about how to get even with that man, replaying courtroom fantasies and imagining confrontations.

In the months after the disaster, Omar’s memory of the event became fragmented. He cannot put the sequence of being trapped in order: he remembers the first shudders, then suddenly the taste of dust and the sensation of weight on his chest, but the middle is a blank. When the memory does surface—often triggered by an unexpected sound or a graze on his arm—it comes back as a full sensory reliving: the screech of twisting steel in his ears, the smell of concrete dust, the pressure of the beam on his ribs, the panic that he was going to die. These episodes leave him shaking and disoriented, sometimes hours later still checking his surroundings to make sure he is not back in the rubble. After each episode, he was left with the growing conviction that he had been permanently ruined—that the person he used to be had been buried under that concrete beam and had never come out.

Because the full reliving is so terrifying, Omar has developed a set of maladaptive strategies to manage it. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts whenever a memory intrudes—repeating affirmations like “I am safe now”—but this often backfires, making the memory feel more urgent and increasing his anxiety. He also avoids anything medical: hospitals, ambulances, even routine physical exams, because the white walls and antiseptic smell remind him of the emergency room where he was told he might lose his leg. That avoidance has meant he has not had his fractures properly re-evaluated, and he now walks with a slight limp that he tries to hide.

Omar’s threat system is chronically overactive. A sudden movement nearby—a colleague rising from a desk, a car braking sharply—makes him lurch as if bracing for an impact. Unexpected touch, even a hand on his shoulder from his wife, causes him to flinch and sometimes yell out. Before he enters any room, he scans for exits; in meetings he positions himself with a clear line to the door. The threat felt so immediate that he had convinced himself that avoiding all medical settings was justified, even if it meant neglecting his own recovery. This hypervigilance has become automatic, and it feeds directly back into his memory. When he startles, his heart pounds and the sensory reliving often flashes—the shattering of glass, the vibration of rubble—because the bodily alarm state corresponds so closely to the moment of the earthquake. The startle also reinforces his negative appraisals. He has come to believe that he used to be a happy person, but now he is always miserable, and that nothing good can happen to him anymore. He thinks, “Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation—someone smarter or stronger would have escaped earlier.” That self-judgment made the memory feel more vivid, as if he needed to replay the moment over and over to find exactly where he had gone wrong. These appraisals, in turn, escalate his threat perception: if he is fundamentally broken and disaster-prone, then danger is always waiting around the corner, so he must stay alert.

The revenge rumination also fuels the threat cycle. Imagining getting even with his building manager leads to clenched fists and elevated heart rate, which his brain interprets as evidence of imminent danger. He feels he must be prepared for anything. His forced positive reframing, however, has only deepened his despair: when an intrusive memory hits and he tries to replace it with a cheerful thought, the effort fails, and he concludes that he cannot even control his own mind—another confirmation that he is permanently damaged. This maladaptive loop has tightened over the past year. At work, Omar’s productivity has dropped because he spends so much energy monitoring escape routes and suppressing memories. He has snapped at colleagues who approach him silently. His wife has grown worried: he no longer wants to go to restaurants or public places because he cannot relax, and at home he often sits in a corner chair with a view of both doors.

What finally brought Omar to seek help was a dream two weeks ago in which he saw the concrete beam pinning him again, but this time no one came to rescue him. He woke up gasping, and for half an hour he could not shake the feeling that it was actually happening. That morning he told his wife he would see a therapist, though he is terrified that talking about the earthquake will make the memories permanent and that therapy itself might involve hospitals. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again. What he hopes, but cannot yet articulate, is that someone might help him understand why the world still feels like it is about to collapse, even when everything is standing still.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to or influence the trauma memory.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly leads to negative appraisals about oneself or the world.
No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat directly drives maladaptive coping strategies.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to or influence the trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly leads to negative appraisals about oneself or the world.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat directly drives maladaptive coping strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
